title: Ricardo Rocco Joins Korn Ferry as Senior Client Partner
summary: Ricardo Rocco has joined Korn Ferry as a Senior Client Partner in the Consumer Practice.
body_text: Miami, August 4, 2026 – Korn Ferry (NYSE: KFY) today announced that Ricardo Rocco has joined the firm as a Senior Client Partner in the Consumer Practice. He will be based in the firm's Miami office. Rocco brings more than two decades of corporate leadership and executive search experience across the consumer, beverage, and industrial sectors, advising clients on leadership needs across the Americas and global markets. “We are delighted to welcome Ricardo to our global Consumer Practice,” said Dominique Virchaux, President, Global Consumer Market, Korn Ferry. “His expertise and deep relationships with boards and executive teams will further strengthen our ability to deliver exceptional leadership solutions for clients across the consumer sector.” Rocco holds a Bachelor of Science in Aeronautical Mechanical Engineering from ITA (Instituto Tecnológico de Aeronáutica), Brazil. About Korn Ferry Korn Ferry is a global consulting firm that powers performance. We unlock the potential in your people and unleash transformation across your business—synchronizing strategy, operations, and talent to accelerate performance, fuel growth, and inspire a legacy of change. That’s why the world’s most forward-thinking companies across every major industry turn to us—for a shared commitment to lasting impact and the bold ambition to Be More Than . As the Official Talent & Organizational Consulting Partner of LA28, Korn Ferry is powering the nearly 5,000 people who power the Olympic Games—bringing in the right talent, building strong leaders, and shaping the structure and culture that will deliver an unforgettable experience for the world.

title: Gemini 4 Release Date: What We Know and What's Rumored
summary: No Gemini 4 release date yet. Get the confirmed facts, the Gemini 3.5 Pro delay, and prediction-market odds for a late-2026 launch.
body_text: Google has not announced a Gemini 4 release date, and as of August 2026 the model exists only as a training run. The only official facts come from two statements in late July: a single line at the end of Google's Gemini 3.6 Flash launch post, and a follow-up from CEO Sundar Pichai on Alphabet's Q2 earnings call. Everything else circulating online, including the widely repeated late-2026 window, is inference from Google's past release cadence rather than anything the company has committed to. Here is what is actually confirmed, why a real date does not exist yet, and what the timing signals point to. What Google has confirmed about Gemini 4 Google confirmed Gemini 4 is in pre-training on July 21, 2026. The confirmation arrived at the tail of the post announcing Gemini 3.6 Flash, 3.5 Flash-Lite, and 3.5 Flash Cyber, where the Gemini team wrote that it had "already started our most ambitious pre-training run yet, for Gemini 4." Google AI Studio lead Logan Kilpatrick repeated the milestone on X the same day. Pichai widened the picture two days later on the Q2 2026 earnings call . Asked whether Gemini can stay at the frontier, he said the next generation would need much larger base models and confirmed the model by name: "We are now training Gemini 4, and we're being very ambitious with it." He described the effort as significantly larger than any prior Gemini and named coding and agentic coding as the capability areas Google most needs to improve. One more signal came out of the same call. Pichai said Google intends to move toward an almost monthly release cadence for Gemini models, a shift from its slower historical rhythm. That is the complete confirmed record. No release date, model ID, benchmark, price, context window, or variant lineup has been published. Why there is still no Gemini 4 release date Pre-training is an engineering milestone, not a product. A frontier model has to clear several stages after the training run before anyone outside Google can use it, and none of them moves quickly. Post-training covers instruction tuning, safety alignment, and tool-use integration. Internal evaluation stress-tests reasoning, long-context reliability, and agent behavior. Only then comes limited preview access, and finally general availability with a stable model ID and documentation. Google's own recent history shows how long that gap can run. The confirmation of a training run tells you the next generation is underway. It does not tell you the model is close, and it is not the same as a model page appearing in the API catalog. What the timing signals point to Prediction markets currently put a Gemini 4 launch most likely in late 2026, though the odds fall off sharply before then. On Manifold , the community-run market for a Gemini 4.0 release gives roughly a 74% chance of a launch before November 2026, about 85% before December, and about 89% before the end of the year. Traders price an October arrival at closer to 32%. These are crowd forecasts tied to a defined resolution condition, not insider knowledge, but they track the same late-2026 window that analysts have inferred from Google's six-month development cycles. Tech press estimates land in the same range. 9to5Google reasoned that, based on past releases, Gemini 4 should arrive in November or December 2026. Google has attached no date to that window, so treat every specific month as an educated guess until a model ID appears in the Gemini API or Vertex AI catalog. The Gemini 3.5 Pro delay hanging over the timeline The Gemini 3.5 Pro delay is the reason many developers read the Gemini 4 tease with caution. Google announced the 3.5 series at I/O in May 2026 and said the Pro flagship would follow the next month. It has not shipped. Google now describes 3.5 Pro as testing with partners and says it will launch "as soon as it's ready," and Bloomberg reported that coding performance drove the slip after a late-June training-data update fell short of internal targets. Promoting the next generation before the current flagship reaches general availability is what unsettled parts of the developer community. It also matters for the Gemini 4 timeline: Gemini 3.5 Pro and Gemini 4 are separate models trained in parallel, so a still-unreleased flagship in the current generation is a live signal about how long a finished-looking model can sit before launch. Gemini 4 versus Gemma 4 Gemini 4 and Gemma 4 are different products, and the similar names are the biggest source of confusion in search results. Gemini 4 is Google's proprietary frontier model, unreleased and accessible only through Google's infrastructure once it ships. Gemma 4 is the open-weight family Google released in April 2026, built from Gemini research but downloadable and runnable on your own hardware. Benchmark numbers and specs that surface under a "Gemini 4" search usually belong to Gemma 4, not the unreleased frontier model. What to use until Gemini 4 ships The practical Google options today are the current-generation Gemini models, all available while Gemini 4 trains. Gemini 3.6 Flash is the current workhorse at $1.50 per million input tokens and $7.50 per million output tokens, with stronger coding and agentic benchmarks than the model it replaced. Gemini 3.7 Flash , launched August 13, 2026, sits alongside it. For heavier reasoning and long-context work, Gemini 3.1 Pro runs $2.00 input and $12.00 output per million tokens on prompts up to 200K tokens. High-volume, latency-sensitive jobs can drop to Gemini 3.5 Flash-Lite at $0.30 and $2.50. Pricing is current as of August 2026 and set on the standard paid tier. Waiting for an unannounced model carries a real opportunity cost. Building on a current model now, with a replaceable model layer, lets you switch to Gemini 4 the day it lands without rearchitecting anything. If you would rather build than wait, the model you use should not lock you in. Emergent builds full-stack applications from a plain-language description, and its Universal LLM Key gives you access to Claude, GPT, and Gemini through one credential and unified billing, with no separate API accounts to set up. Emergent supports Google's current Gemini models today, so when Gemini 4 becomes available on the platform, you can start using it without new keys or extra configuration. title: Best creative automation software: 2026 guide
summary: Creative automation software, split into platforms that scale creative and AI tools that generate it, with real pricing compared.
body_text: TL;DR Creative automation software produces and adapts marketing creative at scale, so a small team can ship what once took a studio. In 2026 the category splits in two: platforms that scale and serve creative you already designed, and AI-native tools that generate the creative itself. The best creative automation software for you depends on which of those jobs you are trying to automate. Celtra and Bannerflow are best for enterprise brands and in-house ad teams, because they turn one master design into thousands of on-brand ad versions and serve them across formats, markets and channels. Presti is best for retailers and brands, because it generates on-brand product photography and video at catalog scale, rather than resizing an ad you already made. AdCreative AI is best for performance marketers, because it generates and scores conversion-focused ad creatives and pushes them straight to Meta, Google and LinkedIn. Quick rule: pick a creative management platform to scale and serve creative, and an AI-native generator to create it in the first place. Many teams run both. Two waves hide inside "creative automation" What if one designer could produce a full campaign, in every size, language and channel, before lunch? That is the promise of creative automation software. You feed it a design or a product, and it returns the finished creative in minutes, without a studio, a resizing marathon or a reshoot. The catch is that "creative automation" now describes two very different kinds of tool, and most comparisons blur them into one list. So let us draw the line clearly. The first wave is the creative management platforms , the tools built to scale and serve creative: you give them a master design and they generate every format, version and localized variant, then push those ads out and optimize them. Celtra, Bannerflow, Rocketium and Creatopy (now The Brief) live here. The second wave is the AI-native creative generators , the tools that make the creative itself from a prompt or a product photo. AdCreative AI and Presti sit here. A management platform is the assembly line; an AI generator is the thing that stamps out the first part. The line is blurring, to be fair. The management platforms are bolting on generative AI, and the AI tools are adding resizing and brand controls. But the core job still separates them, and it is the fastest way to shortlist. Presti is our own product and sits in the second wave, so we hold its section to the same factual standard as the rest and are upfront about where it is not the right fit. How we compared these tools We did not run a single scripted benchmark across all six tools, so we do not report head-to-head test scores. Three of the six do not publish pricing at all, which itself shapes the comparison. Instead we compared them on the criteria that decide whether the software fits your job, all read from each vendor's own pages on 13 August 2026. Core job: does the tool scale and serve creative you designed, or generate new creative from scratch? Outputs: display banners, social and video, product visuals, and how many formats and versions it can spin out. Brand consistency: templates, brand kits or a brand-trained model that keeps a large output on-brand. Pricing transparency and real cost: is pricing public, and what does a representative month actually cost, credits, seats and hidden gates included? Commercial rights and integrations: can you use the output commercially, and does it plug into your ad, DAM and workflow stack? We quote standard monthly billing in US dollars; annual plans are usually cheaper. Where a vendor sells credits or per-seat plans, we translate the headline into a rough real cost. Where a vendor publishes no pricing, we say so plainly rather than guess. Creative automation software at a glance Six creative automation tools compared. Standard monthly billing, USD, verified 13 August 2026. "Not publicly listed" = the vendor publishes no pricing and quotes on request. Tool Wave / type Best for Entry price (monthly) Free tier Watch-out Celtra Creative management platform Enterprise brands and agencies scaling ad creative across markets Not publicly listed (custom quote) No Enterprise sales motion; add-ons stack up the bill Bannerflow Creative management platform In-house teams running global display and video ad campaigns Not publicly listed (custom quote) No Display-ad centric; enterprise-oriented Rocketium Agentic creative studio Retail-media and enterprise teams wanting a managed, on-brand pipeline Not publicly listed (custom quote) No Service-blended, not pure self-serve; stats are vendor-reported Creatopy (now The Brief) Ad design + creative automation Solo creators, marketing teams and agencies wanting self-serve ad design Create $39; Amplify $99; Collaborate $59/seat 7-day trial, no card Collaboration, SSO, API and CMYK gated to higher tiers AdCreative AI AI-native ad generator Performance marketers who want scored, conversion-focused ad creatives Starter $39 (10 downloads) Free trial Steep tier jumps; full IP rights gated to Enterprise Presti AI-native product-visual generator Retailers and brands generating on-brand product photos and video at scale Pro $99 (1,000 credits, ~33 videos or ~333 images) Yes, 60 credits Built for product visuals, not ad-format resizing or DCO Wave 1: Creative management platforms: scale and serve the creative A creative management platform (CMP) does not usually invent your creative. It takes a master concept, or a set of brand assets, and industrializes it: hundreds of format and size versions, localized copy, dynamic variants driven by a data feed, plus approval workflows and ad serving on top. This is the older, enterprise-heavy end of creative automation software, where "automation" mostly means production and operations, not generation. The three pure players below quote on request; Creatopy, now The Brief, sits at the self-serve edge of this wave and does publish prices. Celtra Celtra calls itself a creative automation company, and it is built for scale. You start from a master design and Celtra adapts it into thousands of on-brand versions across formats, placements, audiences and markets, with a node-based generative design system, predictive AI that flags likely performance before launch, and Dynamic Product Ads as an add-on. It connects to more than 100 tools, naming Adobe, Google Ad Manager, Meta, The Trade Desk and DAMs such as Bynder. Celtra cites 400-plus creative teams and enterprise names including Nike, Unilever, Spotify, McDonald's and Adidas. Best for: large advertisers and agencies that produce high volumes of on-brand ad creative across many formats and markets. Where it falls short: no public pricing and no self-serve entry; the core platform plus serving volume plus add-ons (Dynamic Product Ads, predictive AI, custom APIs) make total cost hard to estimate up front. It is aimed at ad production, not product photography. Pricing: Not publicly listed. Celtra's pricing page states it builds a bespoke package by platform, team size, creative volume and serving volume, with no tiers or figures disclosed, so budget for an enterprise contract and a sales conversation. Bannerflow Bannerflow positions itself as an AI-powered creative automation platform that runs the whole ad lifecycle, from build to optimization to delivery. Its Creative Studio produces HTML5 display banners, video and rich media, then automates resizing and versioning so one master creative becomes every format you need. It adds dynamic creative optimization, AI-powered translation for multi-market rollouts, and distribution through more than 100 integrations across display, social and DOOH. Bannerflow says it serves 2,000-plus brands and leans toward in-house marketing teams. Best for: in-house marketing and creative teams at enterprise brands running display and video ad campaigns across markets. Where it falls short: strongly display-ad and enterprise oriented, so it is more than a small team or a product-catalog use case needs, and it publishes no public pricing. Pricing: Not publicly listed. Bannerflow's pricing page shows only "custom pricing, tailored to your team's needs" and a book-a-demo call to action, so expect an enterprise quote rather than a sign-up. Rocketium Rocketium now presents as Rocketium AI Studio, an "agentic creative studio" that blends AI agents, brand-trained creative intelligence and human design experts to turn a brief into campaign-ready assets in hours. Its stronger suit is retail media: it builds compliant ads for Amazon Sponsored Products, Walmart Connect, Target Roundel, Instacart and other retail networks, with automated resizing, bulk generation, pixel-level brand-compliance checks, role-based approvals and analytics. Its terms state you own the content you create on the platform. Because part of the offer is human design service, it reads less like a pure self-serve SaaS and more like a managed studio with software underneath. Best for: retail-media and enterprise teams that want scaled, on-brand campaign assets delivered through a managed, agentic workflow. Where it falls short: pricing is quote-only, the service-blended model is not a self-serve tool, and the speed and savings figures on the site are vendor-reported testimonials rather than independent results. Pricing: Not publicly listed. Rocketium's pricing page offers a pilot and a custom demo, with only comparative marketing claims (for example "saves 20%+ over agencies") and no plan figures. Creatopy (now The Brief) Heads up on the name: Creatopy rebranded to The Brief in 2026, and creatopy.com now redirects to thebrief.ai , so you will meet both names while the change settles. The product is a brand-trained AI ad platform that unifies generation, adaptation, publishing and optimization. It pairs an Ad Studio and a Canvas with 5,000-plus templates, a Banner Generator and Feed Ad Builder that spin one design into many formats, a Banner Resizer, and AI image, video, copy and translation tools. It exports HTML5, MP4, PDF and more, serves ads to a large network list and publishes to Meta and Google Ads. Usefully, it drops the credit meter: AI is "included for normal use" on a fair-use soft cap rather than a per-download counter. Best for: solo creators, marketing teams and agencies that want template-based ad design plus generative AI, with transparent self-serve pricing. Where it falls short: the two cheaper plans are single-seat, so collaboration needs the Team plan, and SSO, API, DAM integrations and CMYK export are Enterprise-only. AI is fair-use capped, and the site quotes an inconsistent ad-network count (40-plus on the homepage, 25-plus on the plan rows), worth confirming for your channels. Pricing: On standard monthly billing, Create (Pro) is $39, Amplify (Ultra) is $99 and Collaborate (Team) is $59 per seat, with Scale (Enterprise) on a custom quote; annual billing is cheaper (roughly $29, $79 and $49 per seat equivalent). Every plan includes a 7-day free trial with no card. Because it is plan-based, not credit-based, the real cost is predictable: a solo marketer pays $39 a month for the generation and export tools. ‍ Wave 2: AI-native generators: create the creative itself The second wave starts one step earlier. Instead of scaling a design you already made, these tools generate the creative from a prompt, a brand or a product photo. That makes them the answer when the bottleneck is not "resize this into 40 sizes" but "we have nothing to resize yet." The two below take that idea in different directions: AdCreative AI toward performance ad creatives, and Presti toward product photography and video. AdCreative AI AdCreative AI generates conversion-focused ad creatives, banners, texts, product photoshoots and videos, and layers data on top. Its Creative Scoring AI predicts a performance and awareness score for each asset, and it can learn from your connected Meta, Google and LinkedIn accounts, while a Competitor Insights feature surfaces rivals' ads. You generate freely and spend a credit only when you download a creative, so the real unit is a finished download, not a render. Now an Appier group company, it is squarely a performance-marketing tool rather than a general design suite. Best for: performance marketers and agencies that want net-new ad creatives with a predicted performance score and one-click publishing to ad platforms. Where it falls short: the tier jumps are steep, full asset IP rights and "commercially safe" models are called out specifically under Enterprise, and lower tiers are tight on brands and seats (Starter is one brand, one user). Credits renew monthly, so confirm rollover before you rely on it. Pricing: On standard monthly billing, Starter is $39 for 10 credits (downloads), Professional is $249 for 50, Ultimate is $999 for 100, and Enterprise is custom; higher credit sub-tiers sit within each plan. Annual billing runs about 50% cheaper. Because a credit equals a download and generation is unlimited, cost per usable creative depends on how many you actually export. Presti Full disclosure: Presti is our own tool. We hold this section to the same factual standard as the others, quote the same public pricing, and are upfront about where it is not the right fit. Presti is our AI visual production platform for product photography and video. You give it a product photo, and an agent plans, generates and delivers the visuals: studio-quality packshots, lifestyle staging, 360° spins, close-ups, product swaps, variants, lighting control, infographics and image-to-video . A Brand Skill encodes your visual identity once, so a large catalog stays on-brand across campaigns. Like several tools here, Presti routes each task to a fitting engine rather than locking you to one; its site names Gemini, GPT Image, Veo, Flux, Kling, Seedance and Grok. The workspace adds roles, in-context comments and approval flows, and Enterprise adds API access and custom integrations. Named customers on its site include Wethenew, Creative Co-Op, JJA Group, But, Ashley and Wayfair. Best for: retailers, marketplaces and brands that need on-brand product photos, 360° spins and video at catalog scale, with team review built in. Where it falls short: Presti generates product visuals; it is not a display-ad CMP, so it does not do banner resizing, dynamic creative optimization or ad serving the way Celtra or Bannerflow do. You also budget in credits, and for a single hero campaign art-directed pixel by pixel, a traditional studio shoot still has the edge. Pricing: A free plan gives 60 credits a month, about 20 images or 2 videos. Pro is $99 a month for 1,000 credits, with an image at 3 credits and a video at 30, so roughly 333 images or 33 videos, near $0.10 an image or $3 a video if you spend on one type, with credit rollover. Enterprise moves to volume pricing from $0.20 per credit (large minimums) with SSO, API access and custom integrations. Output resolution and maximum video length are not stated on the pricing page, so confirm them for your use case. Which creative automation software should you choose Start with the job, not the logo. Are you scaling creative you already have, or making it in the first place? Choose a creative management platform to industrialize ad production. Celtra suits large advertisers scaling on-brand creative across markets, Bannerflow suits in-house teams running global display and video, and Rocketium suits retail-media teams that want a managed, agentic pipeline. All three quote on request. Choose Creatopy (now The Brief) if you want that scale-and-serve workflow with transparent, self-serve pricing from $39 a month, plus generative AI built in. Choose an AI-native generator when the creative does not exist yet. AdCreative AI is the pick for scored, conversion-focused ad creatives, and Presti is the pick for on-brand product photography and video at catalog scale. Whichever wave you land in, test it on your own brand and products first. Fidelity, the formats you actually publish, and commercial rights matter more than any headline feature. And do not assume you need only one: plenty of teams generate with an AI-native tool, then scale and serve through a management platform. For the bigger picture, see our guide of the best AI image to video generators.

title: How Much Does Wegovy Cost for Teens? A Parent's Guide to GLP-1 Costs and Coverage
summary: How much does Wegovy cost for teens? See self-pay prices, why insurance often denies it, and how to compare every cost path for your teen's GLP-1.
body_text: Medically Reviewed by: Dr. Makia Powers, MD, MPH, MSc, DABOM (Diplomate, American Board of Obesity Medicine) Last reviewed: August 2026 Wegovy's price for a teen depends on your insurance, which savings program you use, and whether you are a new patient. As of mid-2026, families paying without insurance spent roughly $199 to $349 a month through Novo Nordisk's own programs — the $199 end is a new-patient promotional rate for the first two fills, while the standard price is about $349. The list price is much higher, close to $1,349 a month. Insurance coverage for teens is limited, so the real cost varies a lot from family to family. Key Takeaways Wegovy is FDA-approved for teens ages 12 and older who have obesity. It has carried this approval since December 2022. Without insurance, the price changes over time. As of mid-2026, Novo Nordisk's own programs ran about $199 to $349 a month — the $199 rate is a new-patient offer for the first two fills, while the standard price is about $349. The list price was about $1,349 a month. Insurance coverage for a teen's weight-management medicine is limited and uneven. Many families face prior authorization or outright denials. Medicare does not pay for weight-loss drugs by law. Medicaid coverage depends on your state. As of January 2026, only 13 state Medicaid programs covered GLP-1 drugs for obesity. A 2025 preprint analysis (not yet peer-reviewed) found that fewer than 1 in 100 teens with obesity were prescribed a GLP-1. That signals how hard these medicines are to access today. The cheapest path is not always the best one. Leading pediatric guidelines say weight-management medicine should be one part of a full care program, not a drug handed over alone. Blueberry Balance costs $149 a month for clinical care: physician visits, dietitian visits, health coaching, and labs. Balance primarily prescribes the Wegovy injection, and that medication is a separate cost: about $199 a month for new patients (first two fills, through December 31, 2026), then about $349 a month at the standard self-pay price (verify current prices on novocare.com). The program fee and the medicine are two different bills. Wondering if Blueberry Balance fits your teen? Check your teen's eligibility Is Wegovy approved for teens? Yes. Wegovy is FDA-approved for teens ages 12 and older who have obesity. A GLP-1 is a class of weight-management medicines that work with your body's own hunger signals to lower appetite. Wegovy (the brand name for semaglutide) won FDA approval for this age group in December 2022. The approval is for teens with obesity, which doctors define as a body mass index (BMI) at or above the 95th percentile for a child's age and sex. In plain terms, that means a teen's BMI falls in the top 5 percent compared with other kids the same age and sex. Wegovy is one of two GLP-1-class medicines approved for this age group: Wegovy (semaglutide): a weekly injection, approved for ages 12 and older. Saxenda (liraglutide): a daily injection, approved for ages 12 and older since December 2020. One drug you may have heard of is not approved for teens. Zepbound (tirzepatide) is approved only for adults. Its label states that safety and effectiveness have not been established in patients under 18. A study in teens is underway, but for now Zepbound is not an option for this age group. These medicines are prescription-only. A teen should start one only after a full evaluation by a doctor who treats childhood obesity. How much does Wegovy cost for teens without insurance? Without insurance, Wegovy's self-pay price runs roughly $199 to $349 a month through Novo Nordisk's own programs, and it changes over time. The $199 end is a new-patient promotional rate for the first two fills; most families pay about $349. The price depends on which program you use and whether you are a new patient, and the $199 promotional rate in particular applies only to a new patient's first two fills at the starter doses (0.25 mg and 0.5 mg). The table below shows Novo Nordisk's official self-pay prices, offered through Novo Nordisk's patient-support program NovoCare, as of August 2026. Treat these as a snapshot, not a promise. The maker can change or cancel any of these offers, and several have set expiration dates. Wegovy dose Self-pay price (as of August 2026) Notes Injection pen, standard self-pay About $349 a month Standard program price Injection pen, starter doses for new patients About $199 a month New patients only, first 2 fills; runs through Dec 31, 2026 List price before any discount About $1,349 a month What the drug "costs" before programs and discounts Two points often confuse families: List price is not what you pay. You may see "$1,349 a month" quoted online. That is the sticker price. Almost no one paying cash pays that amount, because the maker's self-pay programs bring it down a lot. A savings card is not the same as self-pay. Novo Nordisk offers a savings card that can drop the cost to as little as $25 a month. But that card requires private (commercial) insurance and excludes people on government plans. So a teen on Medicaid or CHIP cannot use it. If you have no insurance, the cash route is the self-pay price above, not the $25 card. Because these numbers move, check the official price on novocare.com before you make a decision. The dollar figures here reflect August 2026 and can change. Does insurance cover Wegovy for teens? Sometimes, but coverage for a teen's weight-management medicine is limited and varies a lot by plan. Many families are denied or face heavy paperwork first. Why pediatric GLP-1 coverage is so limited Weight-loss medicines sit in a benefit category that many health plans treat as optional. Large employer plans and marketplace (ACA) plans often exclude or restrict them for obesity. Even when a plan does cover the drug, it usually requires prior authorization first. Prior authorization is when your insurer must approve a medicine before they will pay for it. For a teen, that often means the doctor has to send proof of the diagnosis and supporting records, and the plan can still say no. How rare is access in practice? A 2025 analysis of electronic health records found that fewer than 1 in 100 teens with obesity were prescribed a GLP-1. The study also found teens on Medicaid or paying cash were far less likely to get one than teens with private insurance. The authors tie this partly to coverage limits and prior-authorization rules. This study is a preprint, meaning it has not yet finished peer review. Read it as a signal of how hard access is, not as a coverage rate. Medicaid, Medicare, and marketplace plans Public coverage depends heavily on who pays and where you live: Medicare: By law, Medicare does not pay for drugs used for weight loss. This rarely affects teens, since Medicare mainly covers people 65 and older. We mention it only because "the government won't pay" is a common myth, and the rule that creates it is a Medicare rule. Medicaid: States choose whether to cover weight-loss drugs. As of January 2026, only 13 state Medicaid programs covered GLP-1 drugs for obesity. The rest did not, though they still cover these drugs for other approved uses like diabetes. A special rule for kids on Medicaid: A federal benefit called EPSDT can require Medicaid to cover care that is medically necessary for a child, even when the same benefit is optional for adults. This can help a teen's case. But it is not a guarantee. States and their plans still apply medical-necessity rules, step therapy, and prior authorization, so families may still face denials. The honest takeaway: do not assume coverage. Call the number on your insurance card and ask directly whether your plan covers Wegovy for a teen, and what steps are required. What are the ways families pay for a teen's GLP-1? Families usually pay one of four ways: through insurance (if approved), through cash self-pay, with a savings card (private insurance only), or through a comprehensive care program that bundles the clinical support around the medicine. Here is how those paths compare. Cost path Typical monthly cost What's included Coverage certainty Best for Insurance-covered (if approved) Your copay, which varies Medicine only Low and uncertain for teens; verify with your plan Families whose plan covers an adolescent GLP-1 Cash self-pay through the maker About $199 to $349 (changes over time) Medicine only Not insurance-based Families paying out of pocket with no clinical wraparound Manufacturer savings card As little as $25 Medicine only Requires private insurance; excludes Medicaid and CHIP Families with commercial insurance that already covers it Blueberry Balance program $149 for the program, plus the Wegovy injection from about $199 to $349 a month separately (the $199 rate is a new-patient offer for the first two fills; the standard price is about $349) Physician, dietitian, coaching, and labs (medicine is a separate cost) Predictable program fee; Balance helps navigate drug coverage Families who want care plus cost guidance when coverage is uncertain Notice that the first three paths pay for the medicine only. None of them include the clinical care that helps a teen use the medicine safely and well. How does a comprehensive program like Blueberry Balance compare? A comprehensive program wraps medical care, nutrition support, and monitoring around the medicine, which matches what pediatric guidelines recommend. The American Academy of Pediatrics (AAP) is clear on this. Its 2023 guideline for treating childhood obesity says weight-management medicine should be an adjunct to intensive health behavior and lifestyle treatment, not a standalone fix. In plain language, the medicine works best as one part of a broader plan that includes nutrition, behavior support, and regular follow-up with a care team. Pediatricians ... should offer adolescents 12 years and older with obesity weight loss pharmacotherapy ... as an adjunct to health behavior and lifestyle treatment. American Academy of Pediatrics, 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline (Key Action Statement 12) That guideline is exactly the gap a medicine-only path can leave open. A cash prescription gets you the drug. It does not get you the dietitian, the dose monitoring, or the follow-up visits that help a teen succeed and stay safe. A medicine-only price also tends to hide real costs. Here is what is often left out. What a medicine-only price often leaves out Why it matters Lab work Doctors check labs before and during treatment to monitor health and safety. Dietitian support Nutrition guidance is a core part of the AAP-recommended plan, not an extra. Follow-up visits Regular check-ins track progress, side effects, and whether the dose is working. Dose changes over time These medicines usually start low and step up, which means more visits and adjustments. Blueberry Balance is built to fill that gap. The Balance subscription is $149 a month and includes physician visits, dietitian visits, health coaching, and labs. Nutrition coaching from a registered dietitian is built into the program, so families do not have to find one on their own. Balance primarily prescribes the Wegovy injection, and that medication is a separate cost: about $199 a month for new patients (first two fills, through December 31, 2026), then about $349 a month at the standard self-pay price (verify current prices on novocare.com). Balance fills these prescriptions primarily through NovoCare's mail-order pharmacy. The cost also depends on your insurance or prior-authorization outcome. The program fee and the medicine are two different bills, never one combined price. To be honest about it, Balance is not always the cheapest path. For a family whose insurance fully covers the GLP-1, paying through that plan may cost less. Balance is built for families who want medicine plus clinical care plus help navigating coverage in one place, especially when coverage is uncertain. Want predictable care and cost guidance for your teen? See if Balance fits your family Which cost path is right for your family? The right path depends on your insurance, your budget, and how much support you want around the medicine. A few simple guideposts: If your plan clearly covers it: Paying through insurance may be your lowest-cost option. Confirm the copay and any prior-authorization steps first. If you have private insurance but are not sure about coverage: Ask your plan directly, and ask the prescriber's office to help with prior authorization. If you have no coverage or keep hitting denials: A comprehensive program can remove the guesswork by bundling the care and helping you navigate the drug cost. If cost is your only concern and you already have a care team: A maker's self-pay program may be the simplest route, as long as you understand the price can change. There is no single best answer for every family. The best path is the one that keeps your teen safe, supported, and able to stay on track. When to talk to a doctor about GLP-1s for your teen Talk to a doctor if your teen has obesity and you are weighing a GLP-1, especially if you have already been told the medicine could help. A good first step is a full evaluation with a doctor who treats childhood obesity. They can confirm whether a GLP-1 fits your teen, explain the risks and benefits, and start the insurance process. In our experience caring for Balance families, one of the most common questions parents ask is, "My teen's doctor recommended a GLP-1, but our insurance denied it, so what do we do now?" A denial is often the starting point, not the end of the road. The care team can file an appeal with added medical detail, which sometimes changes the answer. These are prescription medicines Wegovy and Saxenda require a prescription and ongoing medical supervision. Do not buy GLP-1 medicines from unverified online sellers, and do not start, stop, or change a dose without your doctor. These medicines carry a boxed warning about a rare thyroid tumor risk and should not be used by anyone with a personal or family history of medullary thyroid cancer or MEN 2. Call your doctor promptly if your teen has any concerning symptoms while on a GLP-1, such as severe belly pain, repeated vomiting, or signs of an allergic reaction. When in doubt, reach out to your care team. Frequently Asked Questions Is Wegovy FDA-approved for teenagers, and at what age? Yes. Wegovy is approved for teens ages 12 and older who have obesity (a BMI at or above the 95th percentile for age and sex). It has held this approval since December 2022. How much does Wegovy cost per month for a teen without insurance? As of mid-2026, Novo Nordisk's self-pay programs ran roughly $349 a month at the standard self-pay price, or about $199 for a new patient's first two fills (a promotional rate through December 31, 2026). The list price was about $1,349 a month. These numbers change, so verify the current price on novocare.com. Does insurance cover Wegovy for adolescents? Sometimes, but coverage is limited and varies by plan. Many plans exclude or restrict weight-management drugs, and most require prior authorization. Call your insurer to ask about your specific plan. Do Medicaid and Medicare cover GLP-1s for teens? Medicare does not cover drugs for weight loss by law, and it rarely applies to teens anyway. Medicaid depends on your state; as of January 2026, only 13 state programs covered GLP-1 drugs for obesity. A federal rule called EPSDT can help a child's case but does not guarantee approval. Can teens use a manufacturer savings card? Only if they have private (commercial) insurance. The savings card excludes people on government plans, so a teen on Medicaid or CHIP cannot use it. Is the cheapest path always the best path for a teen? Not necessarily. Pediatric guidelines say weight-management medicine works best as one part of a full care program with nutrition support and follow-up. A medicine-only path can skip the care that helps a teen succeed safely. Ready to explore comprehensive care for your teen? Check your teen's eligibility A note on costs and coverage This article is for general education and is not medical advice. Prices, programs, and coverage rules change often. Always confirm coverage with your specific plan, and talk with your pediatrician about what is right for your teen. Sources FDA, Wegovy Prescribing Information (pediatric 12+ indication): https://www.accessdata.fda.gov/drugsatfda_docs/label/2026/215256s029lbl.pdf FDA, News release on Saxenda approval for ages 12 and older (Dec 2020): https://www.fda.gov/drugs/news-events-human-drugs/fda-approves-weight-management-drug-patients-aged-12-and-older Eli Lilly, Zepbound Prescribing Information (not established under 18): https://pi.lilly.com/us/zepbound-uspi.pdf American Academy of Pediatrics, 2023 Clinical Practice Guideline (Executive Summary): https://publications.aap.org/pediatrics/article/151/2/e2022060641/190440/ Novo Nordisk / NovoCare, Wegovy self-pay price guide (accessed August 2026): https://www.novocare.com/content/dam/novonordisk/novocare/redesign/pdf/Wegovy_Price_Guide.pdf HHS / ASPE, Medicare Coverage of Anti-Obesity Medications: https://aspe.hhs.gov/sites/default/files/documents/127bd5b3347b34be31ac5c6b5ed30e6a/medicare-coverage-anti-obesity-meds.pdf KFF, Medicaid Coverage of and Spending on GLP-1s (13 states, as of Jan 2026): https://www.kff.org/medicaid/medicaid-coverage-of-and-spending-on-glp-1s/ medRxiv preprint, Prescribing of GLP-1 Receptor Agonists for Adolescents with Obesity and Associated Disparities (2025): https://www.medrxiv.org/content/10.1101/2025.10.06.25337411

title: Cardiac MRI Review: Patients Urged to Seek Advice After NHS Scan Concerns

body_text: Patients who underwent cardiac MRI scans at Royal Derby Hospital between 2013 and 2020 are being urged to seek advice after a review identified concerns involving misreported scans and possible patient harm. Patients who had cardiac MRI scans at an NHS hospital have been urged to seek advice after a major review identified concerns about scan reports over a seven-year period. A review at Royal Derby Hospital examined more than 1,200 cardiac MRI cases involving a radiology consultant between 2013 and 2020. According to documents reported by the BBC and local media, 176 of the patients whose cases were examined had died. In 101 of those cases, the review identified a cardiac MRI scan that had been misreported. The findings have prompted calls for patients who underwent cardiac MRI examinations at Derby and Burton NHS services during the period to find out whether their scans were included in the review. What did the cardiac MRI review find? The investigation began after concerns were raised by cardiology colleagues in November 2020. Documents relating to the review reportedly examined 1,224 cases involving the consultant. Of the 176 patients who had subsequently died, 101 had a misreported cardiac MRI scan identified during the investigation. Importantly, the figures do not mean that every death was caused by an incorrectly reported MRI scan. Of the 101 deaths examined, 48 reportedly had a potential cardiac cause. In eight cases, there was not enough information available to establish what had happened, including cases where clinical notes were incomplete or the circumstances surrounding the death were unclear. The review also identified cases where patients had experienced harm. Three patients were reportedly found to have suffered moderate harm, while other cases involved what was described as real harm that could potentially have lasting consequences. The trust said the review assessed physical harm and did not examine psychological harm, including the possible emotional consequences of a misdiagnosis or delayed diagnosis. Why are patients being asked to come forward? Solicitors representing people who may have been affected have urged former patients to seek advice if they underwent a cardiac MRI at Royal Derby Hospital during the period covered by the investigation. The reason for the advice is that some patients may not yet have been contacted directly about the review. Medical imaging can play an important role in diagnosing heart conditions and deciding what treatment a patient may need. If a scan is incorrectly interpreted, there can potentially be consequences for a person's diagnosis, monitoring or treatment. However, an incorrectly reported scan does not automatically mean that a patient was harmed or that a medical error caused a particular outcome. Each case needs to be considered individually alongside the patient's symptoms, medical records, subsequent tests and treatment. People who are concerned about a previous scan should therefore seek appropriate medical or legal advice rather than assuming that the review means they were affected. What has the NHS trust said? University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust has apologised to patients and families affected by the findings. The trust acknowledged that the investigation identified a pattern and level of discrepancy that required further investigation and action. It also said that the consultant involved was a trained specialist and that the investigation highlighted wider systems issues rather than simply focusing on an individual. The trust has said changes have been introduced to improve the way cardiac MRI scans are assessed. According to the information reported about the review, cardiac MRI examinations are now routinely assessed by a team involving several cardiologists. The aim is to provide greater oversight and reduce the risk of important findings being missed or incorrectly interpreted. The trust said it was taking the findings seriously and that it wanted to be open about what happened, how the concerns were identified and what had been done in response. What should former cardiac MRI patients do? Anyone who had a cardiac MRI at Royal Derby Hospital between 2013 and 2020 and is concerned about whether their scan was affected may wish to contact the relevant NHS service for information. Patients can also discuss their concerns with their GP or another appropriate healthcare professional, particularly if they have questions about a previous diagnosis or treatment. Those considering whether they may have grounds for a medical negligence claim can seek independent legal advice from a solicitor specialising in clinical negligence. Patients should avoid making assumptions based solely on the reported figures. The review covered a large number of cases, and the circumstances of individual patients varied. If someone believes their health may have been affected by a delayed or incorrect diagnosis, they should explain their concerns clearly and provide as much information as possible about their previous treatment. Why cardiac MRI reports matter A cardiac MRI is a specialist imaging examination that can provide detailed information about the structure and function of the heart. Doctors may use cardiac MRI to investigate a range of heart-related conditions, assess damage and help inform treatment decisions. Like other forms of medical testing, MRI results must be interpreted alongside the patient's medical history, symptoms and other investigations. The Royal Derby Hospital review highlights the importance of accurate reporting, appropriate clinical oversight and effective systems for identifying discrepancies in specialist medical imaging. It also underlines why patients who have concerns about previous medical treatment should have access to clear information about what happened and whether their individual case was affected. A serious review with wider implications The findings from Royal Derby Hospital have raised significant questions about the reporting of cardiac MRI scans during the period under investigation. While the review identified 101 misreported scans among patients who later died, it is important to distinguish an association from proof that an incorrect scan report caused a death. The available information also indicates that the investigation found cases involving potential cardiac causes of death, insufficient information and varying levels of patient harm. The NHS trust has apologised and said lessons have been learned, while changes have reportedly been introduced to strengthen oversight of cardiac MRI reporting. For patients who underwent a cardiac MRI at Royal Derby Hospital between 2013 and 2020, the key message is to seek reliable information if they are concerned. Patients who believe they may have been affected can ask the relevant healthcare provider whether their case was reviewed and seek independent advice about any questions surrounding their diagnosis or treatment. Source: The Sun, reporting published on 19 August 2026, the BBC, Derbyshire Live, Fletchers Solicitors and University Hospitals of Derby and Burton NHS Foundation Trust. Disclaimer: This article is for general information only and does not constitute medical, legal or financial advice. The figures and findings described above are based on reporting and review information available at the time of publication. An incorrectly reported MRI scan does not necessarily mean that a patient suffered harm or that the scan caused a death. Anyone concerned about their individual medical history should speak with a qualified healthcare professional. Anyone considering a potential clinical negligence claim should obtain independent legal advice.

title: How to Learn Regular Expressions: A Developer's Guide [2026]
summary: Learn regex properly: how to read patterns, the JavaScript API, the classic use cases, when regex is the wrong tool, and how to practice in 2026.
body_text: To learn regex, learn to read patterns before you try to write them. Build the syntax up in layers, starting with literal characters and adding character classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups one at a time. Then test every pattern against real strings in a live tester instead of shipping it on faith. Almost nobody does that. The usual approach is to search for "email regex" and paste the first result. It works until it does not, and then there is nothing to debug against. That is the real problem with regular expressions: most people learn them as a lookup table rather than a language. This guide takes the other route, covering the mental model, the syntax, the JavaScript API, the classic patterns, the traps, and the practice loop. What Is a Regular Expression? A regular expression is a pattern that describes a shape of text, used to find, validate, extract, or replace character sequences inside a string. MDN puts it precisely: regular expressions are "patterns used to match character combinations in strings", and in JavaScript they are objects too. Write one as a literal between slashes, or through the constructor when the pattern is built at runtime: const literal = /ab+c/; const built = new RegExp("ab+c"); Regex earns its keep in a few places, and outside them it is usually the wrong tool: Validation. Does this input have the right shape before it reaches your database? Search and replace. Rename a variable across a file, or reformat a thousand dates. Extraction. Pull ticket IDs, prices, or timestamps out of raw text. Log analysis. Filter a million lines down to the fifty that matter. Refactors. Your editor's find-and-replace is the same engine with a UI. How Do You Read a Regular Expression? You read a regex left to right, translating each construct into a plain-English clause and stacking those clauses into a sentence. The syntax is small, and only looks large because it arrives all at once. Learn it in layers. Literals match themselves. Character classes mean "any one of these", so [^0-9] is anything that is not a digit. Quantifiers say how many times. Anchors match positions rather than characters. Groups bundle a sub-pattern so a quantifier applies to all of it. Alternation takes either side of a pipe. And escaping strips a metacharacter of its powers, so \. matches a literal dot. Token What it matches Example [abc] any one character in the set /[aeiou]/ matches a vowel [^abc] any character not in the set /[^0-9]/ matches a non-digit \d \w \s digit, word character, whitespace \d equals [0-9] . any character except a line break /.y/ matches "my" * + ? zero or more, one or more, zero or one /bo*/ matches "boooo" {2,4} between two and four repetitions /a{1,3}/ matches "aa" ^ $ start and end of the input /^A/ matches a leading "A" \b a word boundary, zero characters wide /\bm/ matches "m" in "moon" (x) a capturing group /(\d{4})/ captures a year (?:x) a group that does not capture /(?:ab)+/ repeats without storing Now read one aloud. /^#?([a-f0-9]{6}|[a-f0-9]{3})$/i Start of the input, an optional # , then six or three characters drawn from a to f and 0 to 9, then the end, case-insensitively. That is a hex color validator, and you decoded it without being told what it was. That is the whole skill. Greedy vs Lazy Matching Quantifiers are greedy by default: they take as much as they can, giving characters back only when the rest of the pattern fails. Adding ? makes a quantifier lazy . MDN's example shows the gap: const text = "some <foo> <bar> new </bar> </foo> thing"; text.match(/<.*>/)[0]; // "<foo> <bar> new </bar> </foo>" text.match(/<.*?>/)[0]; // "<foo>" Same string, same intent, wildly different results. When a pattern grabs more than expected, greediness is why. How Do Capture Groups and Backreferences Work? Capture groups store what a parenthesized sub-pattern matched, so you can read those pieces out of the result, reuse them inside the pattern, or reference them in a replacement. Numbered groups arrive in the order their parentheses open: const line = "2026-08-06 ERROR payment failed"; const m = line.match(/^(\d{4})-(\d{2})-(\d{2})\s+(\w+)/); m[0]; // "2026-08-06 ERROR" (the whole match) m[1]; // "2026" m[4]; // "ERROR" A backreference points at a group from inside the pattern itself, which lets a regex demand that something repeat. This one finds accidentally doubled words: /\b(\w+)\s+\1\b/.test("this is is a typo"); // true Once a pattern has more than three groups, counting positions gets miserable. Named groups, added in ES2018, fix that: const iso = /(?<year>\d{4})-(?<month>\d{2})-(?<day>\d{2})/; const { groups } = "2026-08-06".match(iso); groups.year; // "2026" groups.month; // "08" A pattern that reads groups.month instead of m[2] survives its own edits. What Are Lookahead and Lookbehind? Lookaheads and lookbehinds are zero-width assertions: they check whether text appears before or after the current position without consuming any of it. There are four. Following MDN: (?=y) matches x only if x is followed by y, (?!y) only if it is not, (?<=y) only if x is preceded by y, and (?<!y) only if it is not. Lookbehind landed with ES2018 , which is why older tutorials pretend it does not exist. The classic use is a password rule, where several conditions hold at one position: const strong = /^(?=.*[a-z])(?=.*[A-Z])(?=.*\d).{12,}$/; strong.test("correcthorse1"); // false, no uppercase strong.test("CorrectHorse1Battery"); // true Each lookahead scans from the start, confirms one requirement, then hands the position back untouched. Only .{12,} consumes characters. Lookbehind is the mirror image, useful when you want a value but not its marker: "Total: $49.00".match(/(?<=\$)\d+(\.\d{2})?/)[0]; // "49.00" How Do You Use Regex in JavaScript? JavaScript exposes regex through two RegExp methods, test and exec , plus five string methods: match , matchAll , search , replace , and split . Start with test , which answers yes or no: /^\d{5}$/.test("90210"); // true match returns the first match plus its groups, or, with g , a flat array of matches and no group information. When you want both, use matchAll , which MDN describes as returning "an iterator of all results matching this string against a regular expression, including capturing groups". It throws a TypeError without g : const text = "ping [email protected] or [email protected] "; text.match(/\w+@\w+\.\w{2,}/g); // [" [email protected] ", " [email protected] "] [...text.matchAll(/(\w+)@([\w.]+)/g)].map(m => m[1]); // ["ada", "grace"] The most underrated is replace with a function instead of a string. The function receives the match and each capture group, so the replacement can be computed: "Shirt $20, Hat $15".replace(/\$(\d+)/g, (match, amount) => `$${amount * 2}`); // "Shirt $40, Hat $30" What you want Reach for A yes or no answer re.test(str) The first match and its groups str.match(re) without g Every match, flat str.match(re) with g Every match with groups and indices [...str.matchAll(re)] , requires g A transformed string str.replace(re, fn) To break a string apart str.split(re) What Do Regex Flags Do? Flags sit after the closing slash and change how the pattern behaves. g finds every match instead of the first, i ignores case, m makes ^ and $ match at line breaks, s (added in ES2018 ) lets . match line breaks too, u and v switch on full Unicode handling, y anchors matching to the current position, and d reports each match's start and end index. One trap deserves a warning. A regex with the g flag carries a lastIndex property, and test advances it on every call, so the same test against the same string flips between true and false: const re = /a/g; re.test("aa"); // true re.test("aa"); // true re.test("aa"); // false, lastIndex ran off the end That hidden state makes more sense once the language does. This beginner's guide to JavaScript covers the foundations these methods sit on. Which Classic Patterns Are Worth Learning, and Which Are Traps? A handful of patterns come up constantly: emails, URLs, phone numbers, dates, password rules, and pulling values out of prose. One is a trap. Email validation is the trap. There is a persistent belief that a "correct" email regex exists, one implementing RFC 5322 in full. Chasing it wastes an afternoon. The HTML Living Standard declines to try, calling its own definition "a willful violation of RFC 5322" because the RFC syntax is at once too strict, too vague, and too lax for a form field. What browsers run for <input type="email"> is this: /^[a-zA-Z0-9.!#$%&'*+\/=?^_`{|}~-]+@[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?(?:\.[a-zA-Z0-9](?:[a-zA-Z0-9-]{0,61}[a-zA-Z0-9])?)*$/ If the body that writes the web platform spec settles for an approximation, so should you. If your email regex rejects a real address, you have not validated anything. You have lost a user. The only reliable test of an email address is sending mail to it. Validate phone numbers loosely, since formatting varies by country. Prefer new Date() over a date regex, because a pattern can confirm that "2026-02-31" has the right shape but not that it is a real day. Where regex shines is extraction: /\b[A-Z]{2,5}-\d+\b/g pulls every ticket ID out of release notes. When Should You Not Use Regex? Do not use regex on anything with nesting. HTML, XML, JSON, and source code all allow structures inside structures to arbitrary depth, and a regular expression cannot count depth. That is a mathematical limit, not a matter of skill. A pattern that works on your sample HTML is one nested tag away from matching the wrong thing. Use the right tool: HTML in the browser: DOMParser , or query the DOM directly. JSON: JSON.parse . Faster than your regex, and it validates. CSV: a parser that understands quoted fields, since a comma inside quotes is not a delimiter. Source code: your language's AST tooling, which is what codemods are built on. Two heuristics keep you honest. If the pattern is longer than the code it replaces, it is the wrong tool. If you cannot read it aloud in one breath, neither can whoever inherits it. What Is Catastrophic Backtracking? Catastrophic backtracking happens when a regex engine explores exponentially many ways to match a failing input, turning a harmless-looking pattern into a denial-of-service vulnerability. OWASP tracks this as ReDoS and describes the runtime as "exponentially related to input size". When a match fails, the engine backs up and tries a different split of the input, and certain shapes produce astronomically many splits. OWASP's example, ^(a+)+$ , generates 65,536 paths against 17 characters, doubling with each one you add. Not theoretical: on 2 July 2019, Cloudflare deployed a firewall rule containing .*(?:.*=.*) . In their own postmortem , CPU across their global network spiked to nearly 100% and traffic was down for 27 minutes. One regex, one deploy, a worldwide outage. Four habits avoid it: Never nest a quantifier inside a quantified group over an overlapping set. (a+)+ and ([a-z]+)* are the canonical evil shapes. Anchor your patterns. ^ and $ cut off entire branches of the search before it starts. Prefer a specific character class to . , so the engine has fewer places to wander. Never run a user-supplied regex on your server, and cap the input length you match against. How Should You Practice Regex in 2026? Practice regex by writing the test string first and the pattern second, in a live tester that shows every match as you type. Two tools cover most of it. regex101 explains your pattern in plain English as you type, with match details, a debugger, and a benchmark for catching the backtracking problems above. RegExr , built by Grant Skinner's team and open source under GPL v3, is the friendlier of the two for learning. Keep the MDN cheatsheet open beside either. Then the 2026 question: why learn this when AI will write the pattern for you? Because the AI writes it and you own it. Stack Overflow's 2025 Developer Survey found 84% of respondents using or planning to use AI tools, while 45.7% somewhat or highly distrust the accuracy of what comes back, and 66% named "AI solutions that are almost right, but not quite" as their biggest frustration. A regex that is almost right is the purest example: it passes your three test cases and drops one record in ten thousand. Generating regex is cheap now. Reading it, testing it, and rejecting it is not. A roundup of AI coding assistants covers the tools; this guide covers the verification. For a guided start, Scrimba's free Learn Regular Expressions course runs 46 minutes across 34 screencasts, recorded by Beau Carnes and based on freeCodeCamp's Regular Expressions curriculum. It covers the test method, character classes, quantifiers including lazy matching, anchors and whitespace shorthand, lookaheads, and capture groups for search and replace. In Scrimba's scrim format you pause the screencast and edit the instructor's code in the browser, which suits regex better than most topics: the only way to understand a pattern is to change a character and watch what breaks. Being straight about what 46 minutes cannot include: named capture groups and the rest of ES2018, catastrophic backtracking, regex flavors outside JavaScript, and the point where parsers replace patterns. This guide is the map for that half. Three Scrimba courses fill in the language underneath. The free Learn JavaScript course, 9.4 hours with Per Borgen and built with Mozilla MDN, gets strings, arrays, and methods solid. Advanced JavaScript , 9.8 hours with Tom Chant, is the Pro-tier next step. And since regex transfers across languages with small dialect changes, the free Learn Python course, 5.6 hours with Olof Paulson, covers the Python fundamentals you would apply it to, though it teaches core Python rather than regex. Scrimba Pro runs $24.50 per month on the annual plan ($294 per year), with regional and student discounts available. The free courses named here include a completion certificate. The loop matters more than the platform: grab real text, write the pattern, then check it against the cases you expect to fail. For structure around that loop, these guides to free JavaScript courses , coding practice platforms , and learning Python are good starting points. Frequently Asked Questions How long does it take to learn regex? The core syntax takes an afternoon. Character classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups cover most real use, and a focused course gets you there in under an hour. Fluency, reading an unfamiliar pattern without a reference, takes a few weeks of using regex on real text. Is regex the same in every programming language? The fundamentals are. Character classes, quantifiers, anchors, and groups work the same in JavaScript, Python, Java, Go, and command line tools. Dialects differ at the edges: lookbehind support, named group syntax, and Unicode handling vary. Learn one flavor and the rest are small adjustments. Should I just let AI write my regex? Use it, but verify it. AI models produce plausible patterns quickly and are genuinely good at this task. They are also confidently wrong in ways that pass casual testing. Paste any generated pattern into a tester, run your edge cases, and read it token by token before it ships. Do I need regex to get a developer job? You will not be hired for regex alone, but you will be expected to handle it. Form validation, log filtering, and search and replace across a codebase all assume it. Interviewers rarely ask for a pattern from memory. They do expect you to explain one. Key Takeaways A regular expression is a pattern describing a shape of text, used to validate, search, extract, or replace inside strings. Learn regex in layers: literals, classes, quantifiers, anchors, groups, alternation, escaping. Reading comes before writing. Quantifiers are greedy by default; adding ? makes them lazy. Named capture groups, added in ES2018, keep patterns readable. Use test for yes or no, matchAll for every match with its groups, and replace with a function to compute the replacement. Never use regex on nested structures like HTML or JSON. A pattern cannot count depth, so use a parser. Nested quantifiers over overlapping sets cause catastrophic backtracking, the ReDoS flaw that took Cloudflare down for 27 minutes in 2019. AI generates regex quickly but is often almost right, which makes reading and verifying it the durable skill in 2026. Sources MDN Web Docs.
